title: Episode 23: GitHub Gists
description: Lightweight code sharing: creating, editing, forking, and embedding Gists.
concepts: What a Gist is: a lightweight way to share code snippets
Public versus secret Gists (secret is not private)
Creating a Gist from the command line with gh gist create
Adding multiple files to a single Gist
Editing and versioning: Gists are Git repositories
Embedding a Gist in a web page
When to use a Gist versus a full repository
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we’re spending time with two GitHub features that are easy to overlook at first, but incredibly useful once you understand where they fit: Discussions and Gists.

[JAMIE]
I’m glad we’re doing both together, because they feel related without being the same. One is about conversation, the other is about sharing small chunks of content.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Think of Discussions as GitHub’s built-in forum space for repositories and organizations. It’s where questions, brainstorming, announcements, community conversations, and polls can live without pretending to be bug reports or feature work.

[JAMIE]
So not everything belongs in Issues.

[ALEX]
Right. And that distinction matters to maintainers. If you open an issue, you’re signaling that there is actionable work to track. Issues imply workflow: labels, assignees, closing states, progress. A discussion, by contrast, says, “Let’s talk this through,” or “I have a question,” or “I want input before we decide what to build.”

[JAMIE]
That sounds kinder to the project, too. A question posted as an issue can create noise.

[ALEX]
That’s the idea. If the answer might be a conversation rather than a fix, Discussions is often the better home.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Before we go further, one administrative note for workshop alumni. If you’re using the support hub after the workshop, there are usually three places to know: the support hub home page, the Discussions area for Q and A and community conversation, and the Issues area for trackable support requests.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m new and I need help, what are the first best steps?

[ALEX]
Start by reading the pinned “Start Here” resources in Discussions. Then search existing discussions before opening a new thread. And if you’ve hit a setup blocker or an accessibility blocker, use the issue templates in the support repository so maintainers can triage faster.

[JAMIE]
That’s a good open source habit generally: search first, choose the right tool second, then post.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
For learners using assistive technology, let’s ground this in navigation. In many repositories, the Discussions tab appears in the main navigation bar alongside Code, Issues, and Pull Requests. Keyboard users may use T to move through tab items in GitHub’s interface, or K to move among links and land on Discussions.

[JAMIE]
And inside a discussion thread, replies are often exposed as article elements, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. For many screen reader users, that’s useful because NVDA and JAWS can jump by article with A. The reply editor behaves much like the issue comment editor. You’ll usually enter focus mode to type, and Ctrl+Enter commonly submits.

[JAMIE]
What about low-vision users?

[ALEX]
A few important visual patterns: categories often appear in a side panel that may be on the left or right depending on viewport width. Answered Q and A threads typically show a green Answered badge. Polls display percentage bars after you vote, and those bars rely partly on color fill, so it helps to listen for labels and percentages too, not just look at the bars.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users, the visual organization matters: category labels, pinned items, accepted answers, and upvote controls instead of posting “plus one.”

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s make the issue-versus-discussion choice really concrete.

[ALEX]
Sure. Use an issue when you found a bug, want a specific feature, need to track work, or expect an outcome like fixed, closed, or won’t fix. Use a discussion when you have a how-do-I question, want to brainstorm before filing a feature request, want community input, or want an open conversation that may not have one correct answer.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m unsure whether a feature idea is mature enough, I might start in Discussions under Ideas.

[ALEX]
Perfect example. And there are a few common categories you’ll encounter. Q and A is for support questions where one answer can be marked correct. Ideas is for feature brainstorming. Announcements is for releases, roadmaps, or breaking changes from maintainers. General catches broader conversation. And some communities use Show and Tell for sharing what members built.

[JAMIE]
That category system helps set expectations before anyone even opens the thread.

[ALEX]
Yes. It tells you what kind of conversation a project welcomes in that space.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How do learners actually get to Discussions?

[ALEX]
There are two common paths. From a repository, go to the repository page and look in the main navigation for Discussions. If it’s there, open it. If the tab is missing, that doesn’t mean you missed it. Discussions is optional. Maintainers have to enable it, and not every project uses it.

[JAMIE]
That’s reassuring, because people often assume they’re navigating badly when a tab is simply not enabled.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The second path is from an organization page. Larger organizations may have organization-level Discussions that aren’t tied to one repository. Those are community-wide conversations.

[JAMIE]
So a repo discussion might be about one codebase, while an organization discussion could cover broader community questions.

[ALEX]
That’s a useful mental model.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Once you’re on the Discussions home page, categories become the main organizing structure.

[JAMIE]
What should a screen reader user expect there?

[ALEX]
Each category is typically a section with its own heading. A practical pattern is to jump by heading level, then use link navigation to move among discussion titles inside a category. Many people use 3 to jump to category headings if that matches the heading structure on the page, K to move among links or discussion titles depending on browsing mode and keymap, and Enter to open the discussion.

[JAMIE]
And the side panel?

[ALEX]
That panel often contains all categories with item counts, pinned or announcement items near the top, most active discussions, and tags if the repository uses them. On a narrow viewport it may move to a different side or lower in the reading order, so expect layout shifts at high zoom or on smaller screens.

[JAMIE]
So learners should think in terms of landmarks and headings, not just memorizing one exact visual location.

[ALEX]
Yes. That’s especially important for accessibility.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s walk through creating a discussion.

[ALEX]
From the Discussions tab, activate the New discussion button. Then choose a category, because category selection affects what options and fields appear. After that, enter a title and body, then activate Start discussion.

[JAMIE]
And title quality matters.

[ALEX]
Very much. A clear, searchable title helps future learners and maintainers. “How do I use the daily-briefing agent?” is far better than “Help.” If you’re posting in Q and A, phrase the title as an actual question.

[JAMIE]
What does the screen reader path usually feel like?

[ALEX]
Typically: tab to New discussion, press Enter, arrow through the category list, press Enter to choose one, move to the title field, then to the body editor. Enter focus mode to type or paste content, then tab to Start discussion and activate it. And often Ctrl+Enter submits, just as with issue comments.

[JAMIE]
Before posting, search first.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Use the search bar in Discussions, or GitHub’s global search with a qualifier like repo:owner-slash-name in:discussions. That can save everyone time and keep knowledge in one place.

[JAMIE]
Any low-vision details worth calling out?

[ALEX]
Yes. The category selector may appear as labeled cards or a list with descriptions. At high zoom, take time to read the category descriptions so you choose the right space. Title and body usually stack vertically. After posting, confirmation may appear in a success banner near the top, so if you don’t immediately notice confirmation, scroll back upward.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users, the page often looks similar to opening a new issue, which can reduce the learning curve.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let’s talk about participating once a discussion exists.

[JAMIE]
Reading first, then replying.

[ALEX]
Good order. A discussion page is structured a lot like an issue page: original post at the top, replies below, sometimes an accepted answer pinned near the top in Q and A, and a reply editor near the bottom.

[JAMIE]
How would you navigate it efficiently with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
Jump by headings to move between the original post and reply headings. Some users may use heading navigation at a particular level if replies are marked that way. Then arrow through content to read details. The goal is to avoid linearly reading the entire page if you only need the accepted answer or a specific reply.

[JAMIE]
And to reply?

[ALEX]
Navigate to the bottom reply area, or use a Reply button on a particular comment. The text area behaves like other GitHub comment editors: enter focus mode, type, then submit with Ctrl+Enter or use the visible submit control.

[JAMIE]
What about nested replies?

[ALEX]
Each comment may have its own Reply button. Activating it opens a nested text area under that comment, which helps keep local back-and-forth attached to the right context.

[JAMIE]
That’s useful, especially in long support threads.

[ALEX]
Very. And one more etiquette point: if you agree with a post or want to signal that an answer helped, use the thumbs-up or other reactions instead of leaving a “plus one” comment. Many maintainers look at upvotes to prioritize the most useful answers.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
In Q and A, one answer can be marked correct. How does that work conceptually?

[ALEX]
In Q and A discussions, the discussion author can mark one reply as the accepted answer. When that happens, GitHub highlights it and typically pins it near the top, with an Answered indicator on the thread.

[JAMIE]
That’s huge for accessibility because it reduces scanning.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Instead of reading an entire thread to discover which reply solved the problem, you can often find the accepted answer immediately. To mark an answer as the discussion author, locate the preferred reply and use the control GitHub provides to mark it as the answer. Once marked, it becomes visually and structurally distinguished from the rest of the conversation.

[JAMIE]
And if an answer changes over time?

[ALEX]
The author can usually update which reply is accepted if a better answer emerges. That’s one of the strengths of a living support forum.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now, polls. These surprise some people because they don’t realize GitHub Discussions can do that.

[ALEX]
Yes. In communities that enable polls, they’re useful for quick preference gathering: meeting times, naming choices, roadmap priorities, and similar lightweight decisions.

[JAMIE]
How do you create one?

[ALEX]
You begin a new discussion in a category that supports polls, then add a poll with a question and response options. Depending on the interface and current GitHub behavior, you may also choose settings like whether voters can select one option or multiple. The key concept is that polls belong to discussion workflows, not issue workflows.

[JAMIE]
And voting?

[ALEX]
Open the poll discussion, review the options, select your choice or choices as allowed, and submit the vote. After voting, results are usually shown as percentages and bars.

[JAMIE]
Important reminder for low-vision and nonvisual users: don’t rely only on bar fill color. Listen for or read the text labels and percentages.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s give a focused screen reader navigation reference for Discussions.

[JAMIE]
A kind of practical cheat sheet.

[ALEX]
Yes. On the discussions list page, use headings to move across categories and sections, links to open individual threads, and landmarks to understand where the main content and side content live. Expect a side panel containing categories, pinned items, activity, or tags.

[JAMIE]
And inside a discussion?

[ALEX]
Use heading navigation to locate the title, original post, accepted answer if present, and replies. Article navigation can help move reply by reply. The editor behaves like other GitHub comment forms, so focus mode is important.

[JAMIE]
Any reader-specific notes?

[ALEX]
A few. In NVDA, article navigation with A is often especially handy for moving between replies. In JAWS, A can also help when articles are exposed clearly. In VoiceOver, users may lean more on the rotor for headings, landmarks, links, and form controls rather than using the exact same keystrokes as NVDA or JAWS. The deeper point is not the one perfect command. It’s understanding the page structure: headings, articles, controls, and editor regions.

[JAMIE]
That’s a helpful framing. Learn the structure, then map your screen reader’s commands onto it.

[ALEX]
Precisely.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Tell me more about organization-level Discussions.

[ALEX]
These are discussions attached to an organization rather than a single repo. They work well for broad community support, governance conversation, event planning, or cross-project announcements. If a repo-specific answer would be too narrow, the organization forum may be the better place.

[JAMIE]
So learners should notice the context. A discussion at the organization level may not map to one codebase.

[ALEX]
Correct. And that changes how you write your post. Be explicit about which repository, tool, or workflow you’re asking about if you’re in a broader community space.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There’s also a section about accessibility agents and what’s different here. What should learners understand?

[ALEX]
The big idea is that Discussions is less task-centric than Issues. Accessibility support tools, AI agents, or automation helpers may be less able to infer one concrete next step because the content is conversational. A thread may contain brainstorming, opinion, support, and clarification all at once.

[JAMIE]
So if someone is using an accessibility-focused assistant or any kind of summarizing agent, they should expect ambiguity.

[ALEX]
Yes. Ask for structure explicitly. For example: “List the accepted answer, unresolved follow-up questions, and any commands mentioned.” In Discussions, that kind of prompt can be more useful than “What should I do?” because the thread may not be about a single action.

[JAMIE]
And because accepted answers, pinned posts, reactions, and category context all matter, an agent needs that context too.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s shift to GitHub Gists.

[JAMIE]
The tiny-shareable-content side of GitHub.

[ALEX]
That’s a good shorthand. Gists are for sharing code snippets, notes, small configuration files, examples, or short collections of files without creating a full repository workflow around them.

[JAMIE]
So a gist is not just “a repo with a shorter name.”

[ALEX]
Right. It has overlap with repositories, but the purpose is different. A gist is lightweight and optimized for sharing a small piece of content. It’s often used for examples, scratch notes, demos, reproducible snippets, or config sharing.

[JAMIE]
And for accessibility learners, that can be especially practical. You may want to share one NVDA config excerpt, one Markdown note, or one short script.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What is a gist, technically and conceptually?

[ALEX]
Conceptually, it’s a shareable code or text snippet hosted by GitHub. A gist can contain one file or multiple files. It has a page, a URL, revision history, and options like editing, commenting, forking, and cloning.

[JAMIE]
So it’s still versioned content.

[ALEX]
Yes. It’s lightweight, but not disposable in the sense of losing history. Git underlies it enough that you can clone a gist, edit it, and keep a revision trail.

[JAMIE]
That makes it stronger than pasting code into a generic note tool.

[ALEX]
Precisely.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
When should someone use a gist instead of a repository?

[ALEX]
Use a gist when the content is small, self-contained, and primarily meant to be shared or referenced. A quick code example, a sample config, workshop notes, or a snippet for a Q and A answer are good candidates.

[JAMIE]
And use a repository when the project is larger, needs structure, collaboration, issues, pull requests, documentation, or a meaningful file tree.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If you need branching workflows, maintainers, project organization, tests, releases, or ongoing development, choose a repository. If you just need to hand someone a small, readable artifact, a gist can be ideal.

[JAMIE]
So the question is not “Which is better?” It’s “What scale and workflow does this content need?”

[ALEX]
Well put.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Creating a gist through the GitHub web interface is usually straightforward. Go to the gist creation page, enter an optional description, provide a filename, and add content. Then choose whether to create it as public or secret, and submit.

[JAMIE]
Let’s pause on that filename point. That affects syntax highlighting, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. The filename matters. If you name a file with an extension like .md, .py, .json, or .txt, GitHub can often infer the file type and render or highlight it appropriately.

[JAMIE]
What’s the screen reader experience like?

[ALEX]
Typically there’s a description field, then a filename field, then the editor itself. After entering content, you’ll encounter controls for creating the gist. As with other GitHub editors, focus mode may be necessary to type smoothly in the text area.

[JAMIE]
And people can add more than one file?

[ALEX]
Yes. A gist can contain multiple files. There’s usually an Add file option or similar control on the page. That’s useful if your example needs, say, a README plus a script, or a config file plus a sample output file.

[JAMIE]
So even though gists are lightweight, they’re not limited to one file.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What are the practical learning-card takeaways for creating a gist?

[ALEX]
For screen reader users: expect a filename field and code editor, enter focus mode when needed, and choose a meaningful filename for proper rendering. For low-vision users: the create page can be dense, so zoom carefully and verify whether you selected public or secret before submitting. For sighted users: don’t skip the filename, and remember that multiple files can live in one gist if your example needs context.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once created, can you edit a gist?

[ALEX]
Yes. Gists can be edited, and edits create revision history. That means you can correct mistakes, improve examples, or update notes without losing the earlier state entirely.

[JAMIE]
Useful for workshop materials that evolve over time.

[ALEX]
Very much so.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about embedding a gist?

[ALEX]
A gist can often be embedded in a web page using the embed script GitHub provides. That makes it useful for blogs, documentation, or course pages when you want the content to remain hosted on GitHub but displayed elsewhere.

[JAMIE]
Any accessibility caution there?

[ALEX]
Yes. Embedded code should still be presented in an accessible context. Don’t assume the embed alone makes the surrounding explanation accessible. If the code matters, describe what it does and provide enough narrative so users aren’t forced to parse raw code without context.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And cloning a gist works the way many Git learners would hope?

[ALEX]
Yes. A gist can be cloned with Git using its clone URL. That lets you pull it down locally, edit it, and push updates if it’s yours or if you have the right workflow for a forked copy.

[JAMIE]
So for learners practicing Git commands, a gist can be a tiny sandbox.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It’s a small target for practicing clone, edit, commit, and push.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Forking a gist—how should people think about that?

[ALEX]
Forking a gist creates your own copy so you can adapt or build on someone else’s snippet. That’s useful when you want to preserve the original while making your own changes. It mirrors repository forking conceptually, just at the gist scale.

[JAMIE]
So if someone shares a config example and I tweak it for my environment, I can fork the gist rather than overwriting their version.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How do users find their own gists later?

[ALEX]
GitHub provides a way to view your gists from your profile or gist area. Look for your gist list, where you can review public and secret gists you own. The exact path can vary with interface changes, so it helps to think in terms of profile navigation and gist listings rather than one frozen layout.

[JAMIE]
Any screen reader guidance?

[ALEX]
Use headings and links to scan the list, and listen carefully for filenames and descriptions. Since gist titles are often really filenames or short descriptions, good naming helps future you just as much as it helps other people.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can you discover public gists from other people too?

[ALEX]
Yes. Public gists are discoverable and shareable. You can browse, search, and follow links to examples people have published openly.

[JAMIE]
That sounds useful, but also like a reason to think carefully before publishing.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about gist comments?

[ALEX]
Gists can have comments, which makes them useful for lightweight collaboration or feedback. To add a comment, open the gist, navigate to the comment area, enter your text, and submit just as you would in other GitHub comment forms.

[JAMIE]
So a gist can become a mini conversation space around a shared snippet.

[ALEX]
Yes, though it’s still not the same as full issue or discussion workflows.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
We need to spend real time on security and privacy here.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. This is one of the most important parts of working with gists. Public gists are public. Anyone can access them, and they may be indexed, shared, and discovered by others.

[JAMIE]
And secret gists?

[ALEX]
Secret gists are not truly private in the strong sense people sometimes assume. They are unlisted, meaning they aren’t broadly discoverable in the same way, but anyone with the link can access them.

[JAMIE]
So secret means obscure, not secured.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Never put sensitive data in a gist. Not in a public gist, not in a secret gist. No passwords, tokens, API keys, private personal data, credentials, or confidential information.

[JAMIE]
That warning cannot be overstated.

[ALEX]
It really can’t. Treat gists as shareable publication surfaces. If it would be harmful for the content to leak, it does not belong there.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s ground gists in example use cases.

[ALEX]
One good example is sharing screen reader configuration. Suppose you want to share NVDA settings for navigating GitHub’s web interface. A gist is a tidy way to publish that config snippet so others can review, copy, and discuss it.

[JAMIE]
Another example is a quick Markdown note.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Imagine workshop day one notes in a single Markdown file. A gist can hold that note, preserve revisions, and give you an easy URL to share with classmates.

[JAMIE]
And a classic third example: a code snippet for answering a Stack Overflow question or similar support thread.

[ALEX]
Yes. Instead of pasting a long block of code inline, you can link to a gist that contains the exact example.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we do a quick comparison between gists and repositories?

[ALEX]
Sure. Gists are best for small, self-contained snippets or notes, often with lightweight sharing in mind. Repositories are best for projects, collaboration, documentation, issue tracking, pull requests, and structured development.

[JAMIE]
A gist is lightweight and fast. A repository is fuller-featured and better for sustained work.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If your content is growing branches, documentation, tests, or contributor workflows, it’s probably time for a repository.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And if you no longer want a gist?

[ALEX]
You can delete it. As always, pause before deleting anything you may need later, and remember that content shared publicly may still have been copied or referenced elsewhere.

[JAMIE]
So deletion is not a guarantee that nobody ever saw it.

[ALEX]
Correct.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s close by tying both features together. Discussions helps a community talk without overloading Issues. Gists helps people share small artifacts without building a whole repository.

[JAMIE]
And both matter for accessible participation. Discussions gives structure to support and community Q and A. Gists gives a practical way to share reproducible snippets, notes, and configurations.

[ALEX]
That’s the core lesson. Choose the space that matches the job. If you need conversation, especially open-ended community conversation, look for Discussions. If you need to publish a small piece of code or text, consider a gist. And in both cases, think about accessibility, naming, searchability, and privacy before you hit submit.

[JAMIE]
And one last habit check: search first, title clearly, post in the right place, and never share secrets.

[ALEX]
Perfect ending.

# Appendix U: Discussions and Gists

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 08: Open Source Culture](08-open-source-culture.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 10](10-notifications-and-day-1-close.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: About discussions](https://docs.github.com/en/discussions)

> This appendix consolidates two related community content features: GitHub Discussions (formerly Appendix G) and GitHub Gists (formerly Appendix F).

---

## GitHub Discussions

>
> **Listen to Episode 24:** [GitHub Discussions](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

## Forum-Style Conversations Beyond Issues and Pull Requests

> GitHub Discussions is a built-in community forum for repositories and organizations. It's where open-ended conversations live - questions, ideas, announcements, polls, and community Q&A - separate from the action-oriented world of issues and pull requests.

### Support Hub Onboarding (Recommended For Workshop Alumni)

For ongoing support after the workshop, use:

- Support hub home: [Community-Access/support](https://github.com/Community-Access/support)
- Q&A and community discussion: [Support Hub Discussions](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/discussions)
- Trackable support requests: [Support Hub Issues](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/issues)

Suggested first steps for students:

1. Read the pinned Start Here resources in Discussions.
2. Search existing discussions before opening a new support thread.
3. Use issue templates for setup blockers or accessibility blockers so maintainers can help faster.

### Learning Cards: GitHub Discussions

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- The Discussions tab is in the repository's main navigation bar alongside Code, Issues, and Pull Requests -- press `T` to navigate tab items or `K` to find the "Discussions" link
- Inside a discussion, replies are `article` elements -- in NVDA press `A` to jump between replies; in JAWS use `A` as well
- The reply editor uses the same behavior as issue comments -- enter Focus Mode to type, then press `Ctrl+Enter` to submit

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Discussion categories appear as a sidebar panel on the left or right depending on viewport width -- look for the category list with item counts
- Answered discussions in the Q&A category display a green "Answered" badge next to the title, with the accepted answer pinned to the top
- Polls show percentage bars next to each option after you vote -- the bars use color fill to indicate proportion

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Discussions are organized by category with colored labels -- the sidebar shows all categories and pinned items
- In Q&A threads, look for the green checkmark on the accepted answer pinned above the regular reply timeline
- Use the upvote button (thumbs up) on replies instead of posting "+1" comments -- maintainers often sort by upvotes

</details>

## Table of Contents

1. [Discussions vs. Issues: When to Use Which](#1-discussions-vs-issues-when-to-use-which)
2. [Navigating to Discussions](#2-navigating-to-discussions)
3. [Discussion Categories](#3-discussion-categories)
4. [Creating a Discussion](#4-creating-a-discussion)
5. [Participating in Discussions](#5-participating-in-discussions)
6. [Marking an Answer](#6-marking-an-answer)
7. [Polls](#7-polls)
8. [Screen Reader Navigation Reference](#8-screen-reader-navigation-reference)
9. [Organization-Level Discussions](#9-organization-level-discussions)
10. [Accessibility Agents: What's Different Here](#10-accessibility-agents-whats-different-here)

## 1. Discussions vs. Issues: When to Use Which

**Not every conversation belongs in an issue.** GitHub Discussions exists for the conversations that don't fit:

| Use Issues When | Use Discussions When |
| ---  | ---  |
| You found a bug | You have a question about how something works |
| You want to request a specific feature | You want to brainstorm ideas before filing a feature request |
| There is actionable work to be done | You want community input before deciding what work to do |
| You need to track progress (labels, assign, close) | You want to have an open conversation without resolving it |
| The answer is "fixed" or "won't fix" | The conversation might not have one right answer |

**The signal for maintainers:** A question in an issue is noisier - it implies something needs to be done. The same question in Discussions doesn't trigger workflow automation and doesn't inflate the issue count.

### Common Discussions categories you'll encounter

- **Q&A** - Support questions and answers (one answer can be marked correct)
- **Ideas** - Feature brainstorming before a formal feature request
- **Announcements** - Maintainer posts about releases, breaking changes, roadmaps
- **General** - Everything else
- **Show and Tell** - Community members showing what they built

## 2. Navigating to Discussions

### From a Repository

1. Navigate to the repository
2. There is a **Discussions** tab in the main navigation (alongside Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, Projects)
3. Press `T` to navigate tab items, or `K` to navigate links and find "Discussions"
4. Press `Enter` to open

**If the tab is missing:** Discussions is an opt-in feature. The repository maintainer must enable it in Settings. Not all repositories use it.

### From an Organization

Large organizations can have organization-level Discussions separate from any individual repository:

1. Navigate to the organization page
2. Look for the Discussions tab at the organization level
3. These are community-wide conversations, not repo-specific

## 3. Discussion Categories

The Discussions home page is organized by category. Each category is a section with its own heading.

### Navigating categories

```text
3 → Jump to category headings
K → Navigate discussion titles within a category
Enter → Open a discussion
```

### The side panel (left or right depending on view width) shows

- All categories with item counts
- Pin/announcements section at top
- Most active discussions
- Tags (if the repo uses them)

## 4. Creating a Discussion

1. From the Discussions tab, activate **"New discussion"** button
2. Select a category (required - affects which fields appear)
3. Fill in:
   - **Title** - Clear and searchable. "How do I use the daily-briefing agent?" not "Help"
   - **Body** - Use Markdown. Same editor as issues
   - For **Q&A** category: phrase the title as a question
4. Activate **"Start discussion"**

### Screen reader path

```text
Tab to "New discussion" button → Enter
→ Category list: ↑/↓ to select category → Enter
→ Title field: type title
→ Tab to body: Focus Mode → type or paste content
→ Tab to "Start discussion" button → Enter
```

**Before posting a question:** Search existing discussions first. Use the search bar at the top of the Discussions page or GitHub's global search with `repo:owner/name in:discussions`.

### Learning Cards: Creating a Discussion

**Screen reader users:**

- Tab to the "New discussion" button from the Discussions tab, then press Enter -- the form loads with a category selector first; arrow through categories and press Enter to select
- The title field comes after the category selector -- type a clear, searchable title; for Q&A category, phrase it as a question so it reads naturally in search results
- The body editor is the same as the issue comment editor -- enter Focus Mode to type, use Markdown formatting, and press `Ctrl+Enter` to submit the discussion

**Low-vision users:**

- The category selector appears as a list or grid of labeled options -- each category has a name and description; zoom in to read the descriptions and pick the right one
- The title and body fields stack vertically in a single-column layout -- the form is the same width as the main content area, making it easy to scan at high zoom
- After creating a discussion, a green success banner appears at the top -- scroll up if you do not see confirmation at your current zoom position

**Sighted users:**

- Categories appear as clickable cards or a list when creating a new discussion -- choose Q&A for questions (allows marking an answer), Ideas for brainstorming, General for everything else
- The "New discussion" button is prominently placed at the top-right of the Discussions tab -- the form layout is nearly identical to the new issue form
- Search existing discussions before posting -- use the search bar at the top of the Discussions page to avoid duplicate questions

## 5. Participating in Discussions

### Reading a Discussion

A discussion page is structured similarly to an issue:

- The original post at the top
- Replies in chronological order
- An "Answered" reply pinned to the top (Q&A category only)
- A reply editor at the bottom

#### Navigation

```text
H → Jump between the original post heading and reply headings
3 → Navigate individual reply headings
↓ → Read through content
```

### Replying to a Discussion

1. Navigate to the bottom of the page (or use the "Reply" button on a specific comment)
2. The reply text area behaves identically to issue comments
3. Focus Mode → type your reply
4. `Ctrl+Enter` to submit

### Replying to a Specific Comment (Nested Reply)

Each comment has a **Reply** button below it:

```text
Tab to "Reply" button on the specific comment → Enter
→ Nested text area opens under that comment
→ Focus Mode → type → Ctrl+Enter
```

### Upvoting

Instead of leaving "+1" comments, use the thumbs-up reaction on the original post or replies. Many maintainers sort discussion responses by upvotes to prioritize most-needed answers.

## 6. Marking an Answer

In the **Q&A** category, one reply can be marked as the accepted answer. This is similar to Stack Overflow's "accepted answer" mechanic.

**Only the discussion author and repository maintainers** can mark an answer.

### To mark an answer (as the discussion author)

1. Navigate to the reply you want to mark as the answer
2. Look for the **"Mark as answer"** button below the reply
3. Activate it - the reply is pinned to the top and the discussion shows a green "Answered" badge

**Why it matters:** Marked answers make Q&A discussions into searchable documentation. Anyone who searches for the same question later immediately sees the correct answer without reading the whole thread.

**To unmark an answer:** Activate "Unmark as answer" on the same reply.

## 7. Polls

Some discussion categories support embedded polls. A poll lets you gather structured vote data from the community.

### Creating a poll

1. When creating a discussion, look for the "Add a poll" option below the body editor
2. Type each poll option (up to 8 options)
3. Set poll duration (optional)
4. Submit the discussion - the poll appears inline

### Voting in a poll

```text
Navigate to the poll section
→ Radio buttons or checkboxes for each option
→ Space/Enter to vote
→ "Vote" button → Enter
```

**Poll results:** After voting, percentages appear next to each option. Screen readers announce the count and percentage per option.

## 8. Screen Reader Navigation Reference

### Discussions List

```text
T                     → Navigate tab bar to reach "Discussions" tab
H / 2                 → Category section headings
3                     → Individual discussion titles (h3 links)
K                     → Navigate all links (discussions, categories, pagination)
Enter                 → Open a discussion
/                     → Focus the search bar (if supported)
```

### Inside a Discussion

```text
H                     → Original post heading and top-level reply headings
3                     → Individual replies
↓                     → Read body content
Tab                   → Move to interactive elements (reply buttons, reactions, mark as answer)
Ctrl+Enter            → Submit a reply (when in text area)
```

#### NVDA note

- Browse mode (NVDA+Space) to read the discussion
- Enter application mode for the reply editor
- Discussion replies are `<article>` elements - NVDA announces "article" as you navigate with H

#### JAWS note

- `A` key navigates `<article>` elements - useful for jumping between replies
- Use Forms Mode for the reply editor

#### VoiceOver note

- VO+Right to read through content
- VO+Command+L to list all links (useful for navigating many replies quickly)
- VO+Space on the reply field to enter interaction mode

## 9. Organization-Level Discussions

Some organizations enable Discussions at the organization level, separate from any repository. These work identically to repository discussions but span the whole organization.

Common uses:

- Org-wide announcements
- Community introductions ("Introduce yourself" pinned thread)
- Cross-repo feature brainstorming
- Community spotlights and events

Find them at `github.com/ORGANIZATION/discussions`.

## 10. Accessibility Agents: What's Different Here

Accessibility Agents prompts currently operate on **issues, PRs, and code** - not directly on Discussions. If you want to respond to a discussion using Accessibility Agents:

1. Copy the discussion URL or content
2. Use `/issue-reply` with the content pasted in: the agent will draft a thoughtful, accessible response
3. Paste the result back into the discussion reply editor

This works well for first-response drafts on Q&A threads or community questions in your area of expertise.

## GitHub Gists

>
> **Listen to Episode 23:** [GitHub Gists](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

## Shareable Code Snippets and Notes

> Gists are a simple way to share code snippets, notes, or small files without creating a full repository. Think of them as lightweight, version-controlled pastebins.

### Learning Cards: GitHub Gists

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- On the Gist creation page at gist.github.com, press `D` to jump to the main landmark, then `F` to navigate form fields: Description, Filename, Content, and Visibility buttons
- Your Gists page lists each gist as an `H2` heading with its description -- press `2` or `H` to jump between gists
- Gists are full Git repositories -- you can clone them with `git clone` and edit locally using your usual screen reader workflow in VS Code

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Gist pages use syntax highlighting matching GitHub's current theme -- switch between light and dark mode for comfortable reading
- Public and secret gists look identical on the page; the only difference is the URL visibility -- check the "Create secret gist" or "Create public gist" button label before submitting
- The revision history link appears at the top of any gist -- click "Revisions" to see a diff view of every edit

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Gists live at gist.github.com, separate from regular repositories -- each gist shows a syntax-highlighted code block with filename tabs at the top
- The visibility selector is a split button at the bottom of the editor -- the dropdown arrow reveals "Create secret gist" vs "Create public gist"
- You can add multiple files to one gist using the "Add file" button below the first editor pane

</details>

## What Is a Gist?

A Gist is a Git repository that holds a single file or a small collection of files. Every Gist:

- Has its own URL (e.g., `gist.github.com/username/a1b2c3d4`)
- Is version-controlled (you can see edit history)
- Can be **public** (anyone can see) or **secret** (only people with the link can see)
- Supports Markdown rendering
- Can be embedded in web pages
- Can be cloned, forked, and starred just like repos

**Secret does not mean private.** Anyone with the URL can view a secret Gist. It's just not listed publicly on your profile.

## When to Use a Gist vs a Repository

| Use a Gist When... | Use a Repository When... |
| --------------------  | --------------------------  |
| Sharing a single code snippet | Building a full project |
| Posting configuration examples | Collaborating with multiple people |
| Quick notes or documentation | Need issues, PRs, or project management |
| Sharing logs or error messages | Want CI/CD and automated checks |
| Small utility scripts | Need multiple branches |

## Creating a Gist

### Via GitHub Web Interface

1. Navigate to [gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com)
2. **Gist description:** A short title (e.g., "NVDA configuration for GitHub")
3. **Filename:** Name your file with extension (e.g., `nvda-config.txt`, `script.py`, `notes.md`)
4. **Content:** Paste or type your code/text
5. **Visibility:**
   - Select **"Create public gist"** for openly shareable content
   - Select **"Create secret gist"** for link-only sharing
6. The Gist is created with a unique URL you can share

#### Screen reader navigation

- `D` to cycle landmarks to "Main"
- `F` to navigate form fields
- Tab through: Description → Filename → Content textbox → Visibility buttons

### Adding Multiple Files to a Gist

You can add multiple files to a single Gist:

1. After typing the first filename and content, select **"Add file"** (button below the editor)
2. Repeat for each additional file
3. Create the Gist

**Use case:** Share related config files together (e.g., `.vscode/settings.json` + `.vscode/keybindings.json`)

### Learning Cards: Creating a Gist

**Screen reader users:**

- On the Gist creation page at gist.github.com, press `D` to jump to the main landmark, then `F` to navigate form fields in order: Description, Filename, Content textarea, and visibility buttons
- The visibility selector is a split button -- the main button creates a public gist; Tab to the dropdown arrow next to it and press Enter to reveal the "Create secret gist" option
- Each filename field has a corresponding content textarea directly below it -- after filling one file, Tab to the "Add file" button to add another file to the same gist

**Low-vision users:**

- The Gist editor uses the same syntax highlighting as regular GitHub files -- your current theme applies; increase font size in browser zoom for comfortable editing
- The split button for public vs. secret visibility is at the bottom of the form -- the two options look nearly identical; read the button label carefully ("Create public gist" vs. "Create secret gist") before clicking
- The "Add file" button appears below the first file editor as a small text link -- zoom in to find it; each additional file gets its own filename field and content textarea

**Sighted users:**

- The Gist creation form has three main fields stacked vertically: description at the top, then filename, then a large code editor -- fill all three before choosing visibility
- The visibility split button at the bottom-right has a dropdown arrow -- click the arrow to choose between public and secret; the default (larger) button creates a public gist
- Add multiple files to a single gist using the "Add file" link below the editor -- multi-file gists are useful for sharing related configurations or code snippets together

## Editing a Gist

1. Navigate to your Gist's URL
2. Select **"Edit"** (button in the top-right)
3. Make your changes
4. Select **"Update public gist"** or **"Update secret gist"**

Every edit creates a new revision. Click **"Revisions"** to see the full edit history.

## Embedding a Gist

You can embed Gists in web pages, blog posts, or documentation:

```html
<script src="https://gist.github.com/username/gist-id.js"></script>
```

GitHub renders it as a formatted code block with syntax highlighting and a link back to the Gist.

**Accessibility note:** Embedded Gists are `<iframe>` elements. Screen readers will announce them as "frame" and allow navigation into the content.

## Cloning a Gist

Every Gist is a Git repository. You can clone it:

```bash
git clone https://gist.github.com/username/gist-id.git
```

Make changes locally, commit, and push just like a normal repo.

## Forking a Gist

You can fork someone else's Gist to create your own copy:

1. View the Gist
2. Select **"Fork"** in the top-right
3. GitHub creates a new Gist under your account

**Use case:** Someone shares a useful script, you fork it, and customize it for your needs.

## Finding Your Gists

**Your Gists page:** [gist.github.com/your-username](https://gist.github.com/)

All your public and secret Gists are listed here. You can:

- Search your Gists by filename or content
- Star Gists you want to reference later
- Delete old Gists

### Screen reader navigation

- Each Gist appears as a heading (H2) with its description
- Press `2` or `H` to jump between Gists
- Each Gist has links: "Edit," "Delete," "Star," "Embed"

## Discovering Public Gists

**Browse trending Gists:** [gist.github.com/discover](https://gist.github.com/discover)

See popular Gists by language. Great for finding:

- Useful scripts and utilities
- Configuration examples
- Code snippets for learning

## Gist Comments

Public Gists support comments. Anyone with a GitHub account can leave a comment, making Gists useful for:

- Asking questions about a snippet
- Suggesting improvements
- Discussing implementation details

### To add a comment

1. Scroll to the bottom of the Gist page
2. `F` to navigate form fields → Find the comment textarea
3. Type your comment (Markdown supported)
4. `Ctrl+Enter` or activate "Comment" button

## Security and Privacy

### Public Gists

- Appear on your profile
- Are indexed by search engines
- Anyone can view, fork, and comment

### Secret Gists

- Do not appear on your profile
- Are not indexed by search engines
- Anyone with the URL can view
- Still version-controlled and can be starred

### Never put sensitive data in Gists

- Passwords or API keys
- Personal identifying information
- Proprietary code you don't have permission to share

If you accidentally post sensitive data:

1. Delete the Gist immediately
2. Revoke/regenerate any exposed credentials
3. Remember: Forks and clones may still exist

## Example Use Cases

### 1. Sharing Screen Reader Config

```text
Filename: nvda-github-config.txt
Content:
# NVDA Settings for GitHub Web Navigation
- Browse Mode: Use screen layout (enabled)
- Verbosity: Most punctuation
- Rate: 65%
- Keyboard shortcuts: Use standard GitHub shortcuts (G+I, G+P, etc.)
```

Share the Gist URL with other screen reader users.

### 2. Quick Markdown Note

```text
Filename: workshop-notes.md
Content:
# Workshop Day 1 Notes
- GitHub Flow: branch → commit → PR → review → merge
- Keyboard shortcuts: G+I (issues), G+P (PRs), / (search)
- Always link PRs to issues with "Closes #N"
```

Reference it later or share with workshop participants.

### 3. Code Snippet for a StackOverflow Answer

When answering questions, paste your code as a Gist and link to it. Readers get syntax highlighting, version history, and the ability to fork your solution.

## Gists vs GitHub Repositories - Quick Comparison

| Feature | Gist | Repository |
| ---------  | ------  | ------------  |
| Issues | No | Yes |
| Pull Requests | No | Yes |
| GitHub Actions | No | Yes |
| Projects | No | Yes |
| Multiple branches | No | Yes |
| Revisions/history | Yes | Yes |
| Forkable | Yes | Yes |
| Embeddable | Yes | No |
| Comments | Yes | Yes (on issues/PRs) |

## Deleting a Gist

1. Navigate to the Gist
2. Select **"Edit"**
3. Select **"Delete"** (top-right, after Edit button)
4. Confirm deletion
